title: The city of nine gates
hookLine: King Puranjana moves into a city of nine gates and forgets his oldest friend: avidya, the wrong knowing at the root
carry: avidya: taking what passes for what lasts
tomorrow: the gods win a war and say, we did this. then fire can't burn one blade of grass.

lines: A KING AND A QUIET FRIEND.
cards: Narada tells this one in the Bhagavata Purana. King Puranjana has an old friend who goes everywhere with him, a friend so quiet he is called only the unknown one. But the king is restless.
He wanders the world until he finds a perfect city with nine gates, and a beautiful queen inside. He moves in, marries her, and the friend slips out of his mind.
Then an army arrives at the gates, one the king never planned for.

teach.h: AN ARMY AT THE NINE GATES.
teach.b: The army belongs to a king called Chandavega, and his three hundred and sixty soldiers, some light and some dark, wear the city down.
All those years Puranjana laughed when the queen laughed and wept when she wept, as if her every mood were his. Now the city burns, and he can't imagine himself without it.
In his next life, his old friend finds him grieving and asks: don't you remember me? Then Narada gives the key. The city of nine gates is the body.
The queen is the mind. The soldiers are the days and nights. Puranjana is you.

teach.h: THE FORGOTTEN FRIEND: THE LORD WITHIN.
teach.b: And the friend you forgot is the Lord within.

This is the Hindu teaching of avidya, ignorance, and Patanjali defines it in sutra 2.5 as four mix-ups: the passing taken as permanent, the impure as pure, what brings pain as pleasant, and the not-self as the self.
The deepest is the last: taking the body, the moods, the roles for the self, when the self is the one living in them.

teach.h: THE FIELD THE OTHERS GROW IN.
teach.b: Sutra 2.4 calls avidya the field, the soil the other afflictions grow in. It isn't a gap in your facts; everyone knows cities fall.
Vidya is knowledge; avidya is its opposite, a wrong knowing that feels true from the inside. The commentator Vyasa compares it to an enemy, not just a missing friend.
Today it looks ordinary: the friend group you assume will always be this close, a bad mood that feels like who you are.
Not a reason for gloom. The friend never left. It's a reason to stop and remember.

how: Narada's story of King Puranjana, in the fourth book of the Bhagavata Purana, is read in Hindu teaching as a map of the self in the body, and Narada explains it himself. In yoga and Vedanta, avidya is treated as the root problem, and students practice discernment, noticing what passes and what remains, as the way to loosen it.

o: a stubborn refusal to learn anything
avidya: a wrong knowing that feels true
a simple gap where facts are missing

games.q: the city and the four mix-ups — tap the pairs.
p: a city sure to stand forever

s: in Narada's story, the city of nine gates stands for the body
Narada gives the key himself: the city is the body, the queen the mind, the forgotten friend the Lord within.
avidya means simply not knowing something
it's a wrong knowing, the opposite of knowledge, not just its absence. everyone knows cities fall.
Patanjali calls ignorance the field for the other afflictions
sutra 2.4: the soil the others grow in.

games.q: Puranjana laughs when the queen laughs, weeps when she weeps, and forgets the friend who was always with him. which mix-up of 2.5 runs deepest here?
o: the not-self taken as the self.
none: he just has a bad memory.
games.why: the city is the body and the queen the mind, Narada says, and Puranjana took them for himself. avidya isn't a missing fact; it's a wrong knowing.

practice: Notice something in you that feels permanent right now, a mood, a worry, a sense of who you are today, and ask it the question Puranjana forgot to ask: has this always been here, and will it always be?
Watch it for a few breaths and see whether it shifts. Then notice what has been watching it the whole time, and rest there. If you pray, let that be a quiet hello to the friend within.

wordCard.voice: Ignorance. Avidya: not a lack of facts but a wrong knowing, taking the passing for the permanent, the painful for the pleasant, the not-self for the self.

orig.note: Sanskrit avidyā: ignorance, wrong knowing; a- (not) + vidyā (knowledge). the field for the other afflictions.

carryVoice: Your line: avidya, taking what passes for what lasts. Puranjana's mistake, and everyone's. Day four hundred forty-nine, done.
